analysis.title: From prompts to power: Generative AI and implications for data centre demand
key_insights: Macquarie models generative AI electricity demand bottom-up from usage (users, prompts, tokens, energy per token) and training compute spend, rather than from supply signals such as chip shipments, power contracted or building pipelines. Supply-side estimates measure commitment, not consumption, so they cannot say whether the build-out is ahead of demand.

Base case generative AI electricity use rises from about 91 TWh in 2025 to roughly 857 TWh in 2040, a more than ninefold increase or about 16.1% a year, even with significant hardware and software efficiency gains modelled. Low case is 464 TWh (about fivefold) and high case is 1,219 TWh (thirteenfold).

Average continuous draw rises from about 10 GW today to 53 GW (low), 98 GW (base) and 139 GW (high) by 2040. Generative AI reaches 2.2% of global electricity in the base case, 1.2% in the low case and 3.1% in the high case, per the table (text elsewhere says about 3%).

Building the data centre and power infrastructure requires about $4.5 to $5.6 trillion by 2040, or $300 to $375 billion a year. The base case implies about 120 GW of installed data-centre capacity by 2040, roughly 106 GW more than today. About 40% of the cost is the facility, generation and grid, and 60% is IT equipment. The figure excludes IT equipment turnover, so it likely understates the total.

Intensity of use drives growth more than headcount. Of the 399-fold rise in tokens from 2025 to 2040, more users contribute 4.8x and more tokens per user per day contribute 83.2x. The heavy-user segment is 5% of users in 2025 and just over 60% of inference energy, rising to a quarter of users and 70% of energy by 2040.

Agentic AI removes the ceiling that human attention places on output length. A heavy user in the base case generates about 3.9 million output tokens a day by 2040, about 190 hours of reading. Microsoft reports 2.3 million GitHub pull requests associated with AI agents in March 2026, a 28-fold rise in ten months.

Efficiency is the largest sensitivity. One percentage point a year of hardware or software efficiency moves 2040 demand by 13% to 17%. Shifting 1% of users from casual to heavy (about 64 million people) moves it 2.3%, while adding 1% of the world population as new users moves it 1.2%.

Efficiency gains are large but outrun by volume. Energy per output token falls about 21-fold net (125-fold from hardware and software alone), and electricity per unit of AI output falls about 28-fold including data-centre overhead. Token volume rises 399-fold, so text inference power rises fourteenfold and total demand ninefold. The paper frames this as the Jevons paradox.

Inference rises from under 60% (57%) of generative AI demand today to about 87% by 2040 in the base case, and between 82% and 89% across scenarios. Inference load follows the working day and week, so it is more predictable but less flexible. Training can be queued but its draw is erratic. Training retains the largest share in the high case.

Training electricity is modelled from laboratory compute spend, not compute growth. Base case spend grows about 20% a year to 2030, then slows to about 3% a year by the late 2030s. Training electricity goes from 39 TWh in 2025 to between 52 and 220 TWh by 2040.

Video is a small and uncertain component. It is about 2% of inference electricity today and 2.5% of demand in the base case, under 5% in the high case. Stress tests (3x as much video, half the per-clip efficiency gain) give 70 and 75 TWh versus 22 TWh in the base case. Only both together reach 242 TWh, about a fifth of the total. Per-second video energy estimates differ by an order of magnitude. Generating video per viewer rather than once for many viewers would make the numbers orders of magnitude too low, but nothing suggests that is imminent.

Cross-check against published forecasts: the base case implies generative AI at about 39% of the IEA's all-data-centre electricity forecast by 2030, close to McKinsey's roughly 40% share of data-centre capacity demand (measured in GW, so not strictly like for like).

Grid implications: training concentrates near model developers (mostly the US, with a parallel Chinese ecosystem), while inference follows users and data-sovereignty rules, so it is likely to be more geographically dispersed, including Europe and other regulated markets. The binding constraint is where load lands, how fast it connects and whether firming and transmission arrive with it, not total generation.

Agentic use could break inference's link to human behaviour in level and shape. Unattended work has no reason to follow the working day, which could flatten the load profile and raise utilisation. Price signals would do much of that on their own, and where load cannot be steered, flexibility can be built through on-site generation, storage or connections sized for swings. Providers already discount deferrable work (OpenAI and Anthropic halve batch prices for 24-hour turnaround) and Google has written about 1 GW of demand response into contracts with five US utilities.

Limitations: energy per token is inferred rather than metered, with roughly a factor-of-two uncertainty common to all scenarios. The model has no economic layer, so it does not test whether the use will be paid for. The Low to High range is an envelope, not a confidence interval, and a true upper bound (heavy use with slow efficiency) is not modelled. Generative AI will get harder to separate from other data-centre demand as it is embedded in software.

sector_views.rationale: Demand-based modelling shows generative AI electricity use rising ninefold by 2040 in the base case, requiring $4.5-5.6 trillion of data centre and power build-out. Even the low case rises about fivefold, so the paper views the demand as large and durable.

risk_factors: Oversupply risk: capacity built ahead of demand, which supply-side forecasts (chip shipments, contracted power, pipelines) cannot test.
Permitting and environmental impact may influence the path of build-out.
Grid availability and behind-the-meter solutions raise difficult questions on connecting load where and when it is needed.
Energy per token is inferred rather than metered, with roughly a factor-of-two uncertainty that would move all scenarios together.
The model has no economic layer, so it does not test whether use will be paid for.
Video energy per second is the least settled input, with published estimates differing by an order of magnitude.
Per-viewer video generation would make the video estimate orders of magnitude too low, though nothing suggests it is imminent.
Generative AI is becoming embedded in other software, making it harder to separate from other data-centre demand and to check estimates against published figures.
charts_described: Figure 6 table: Base case electricity demand 91 TWh (2025), 369 (2030), 603 (2035), 857 (2040), CAGR 16.1%. Low 91, 204, 359, 464 and high 91, 493, 804, 1,219.

Figure 8: base case share of users against share of inference energy. Heavy users are 5% of users and just over 60% of energy in 2025, and a quarter of users and 70% of energy in 2040. Casual users fall from 70% to 40% of users and account for just over 3% of energy by 2040.

Figure 11: sensitivity of 2040 demand. Software efficiency 1pp a year moves it +16.6% / -14.1%, hardware efficiency 1pp +15.0% / -12.9%, heavy-user share 1pp ±2.3%, share of world using AI 1pp ±1.2%, requests, output length or energy per token 1% ±0.8%, moderate-user share 1pp ±0.6%.
Figure 16: video stress test. Video electricity is 22 TWh in the base case, 70 TWh with 3x as much video, 75 TWh if per-clip energy falls half as fast, and 242 TWh with both.
Figure 15: token growth decomposition. 4.8x from more users and 83.2x from more tokens per user per day, 2025 to 2040.
Figure 12: energy efficiency of leading AI hardware improving about 1.3x per year from 2016 to 2025 (Epoch AI).
geopolitical: Training concentrates in the United States, with China running a parallel ecosystem.
Data sovereignty requirements and sector regulation push inference serving capacity into the markets it serves, including Europe and other regulated markets.
In China, more than 95% of the 128,000 micro-dramas launched in Q1 2026 were AI-generated.

tension_points.bull_case: Bottom-up modelling from usage shows generative AI electricity demand rising ninefold by 2040 in the base case and about fivefold even in the low case, growing every year. The load is described as large and durable, and efficiency gains have historically stimulated more demand (Jevons paradox).
tension_points.bear_case: Supply-side forecasts measure commitment rather than consumption, so a build-out could run ahead of demand. Generative AI is the volatile part the capital is exposed to. The model has no economic layer and does not test whether use will be paid for. Energy per token carries a factor-of-two uncertainty.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Adoption stalling at 55% of the world with light use and agentic use spreading slowly, per the low case, which still shows roughly fivefold growth. Efficiency improving faster than modelled would also cut the requirement, since one point a year moves 2040 demand by 13% to 17%.

theme_stances.key_argument: Bottom-up modelling of usage shows generative AI electricity demand growing ninefold by 2040 even with large efficiency gains, requiring $4.5 to $5.6 trillion of data centre and power build-out.
theme_stances.evidence: Our bottom-up work leads us to conclude that the growth will be significant and real.

theme_stances.key_argument: Demand growth is driven far more by intensity of use than breadth of take-up, with heavy and increasingly agentic users carrying most inference load.
theme_stances.evidence: Demand growth is driven far more by intensity of use than breadth of take-up.

theme_stances.key_argument: Inference follows users on a steady daily and weekly rhythm, so the load is more predictable but less flexible, making siting and connection the harder problem than generation.
theme_stances.evidence: the load becomes more predictable but less flexible as it grows larger
